title: Effects of long-term exposure to four widely used drinking water regimens on growth performance and fecal microbiota in C57BL/6J mice
content:
by Mingming Pan, Yanhua Shen, Zhihao Wu, Guiping Wang, Jing Wang, Zhengyu Zhou

Gut microbiota plays a vital role in regulating host physiological status and is susceptible to environmental factors, including different drinking water regimens. This study aimed to explore the effects of long-term exposure to four commonly used drinking water regimens on growth performance and fecal microbiota in C57BL/6J mice. A total of 32 male mice were randomly divided into four groups and continuously administered reverse osmosis water (ROW), hydrochloric acid-acidified water (HCl-AW), sulfuric acid-acidified water (H2SO4-AW), and chlorinated water (CW) for 12 weeks, respectively. Body weight, feed intake, and water intake were measured weekly. After 12 weeks of intervention, fecal samples were collected and subjected to 16S rRNA high-throughput sequencing. Bioinformatic analyses were used to characterize microbial community diversity, composition, and predicted functional profiles. The results demonstrated that the ROW group had the highest fecal microbial α-diversity, while the CW group showed the lowest α-diversity. Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) based on β-diversity revealed clear separation of microbial communities among groups. At the phylum level, significant differences were observed in the relative abundances of Bacteroidota, Firmicutes, Deferribacterota, and Actinobacteriota among all groups. At the genus level, the four drinking water regimens significantly altered the relative abundances of Muribaculaceae, Parabacteroides, Ruminococcaceae, the Eubacterium coprostanoligenes group, Turicibacter, and Bifidobacterium. Functional prediction further revealed significant shifts in multiple microbial metabolic pathways. In terms of growth performance, no significant intergroup differences in body weight or gross weight gain were observed, whereas feed and water intake were markedly altered by different drinking water regimens. In summary, long-term exposure to these four drinking water regimens can profoundly and differentially alter the diversity, composition, and predicted functional profiles of fecal microbiota, and modify feed and water intake in C57BL/6J mice, without inducing significant changes in body weight.
